quote: Despite feedback through a thousand trials, subjects cannot bring themselves to believe that the situation is one in which they cannot predict.
content: With adequate incentives and enough trials they can. When payoffs are made substantial and feedback is clear, the majority of subjects converge toward the maximizing strategy over a few hundred trials (Shanks, Tunney & McCarthy 2002), and the residual matchers are not stupid: matching is what a pattern-detector does, and the subjects who match are the ones who find the pattern when the experimenter secretly puts one in (Gaissmaier & Schooler 2008). In an environment where sequences are usually not random and the experimenter usually has something up his sleeve, continuing to search is defensible for far longer than a thousand trials. The essay calls this "the most important idea in all of rationality"; the literature calls it a strategy that is optimal in some environments and suboptimal in the one Dawes describes.

quote: Decision theory does not burst into flames and die when faced with an opponent who disobeys decision theory.
content: It does not, and what it says to do against an opponent is, very often, randomize. The equilibrium of matching pennies, of rock-paper-scissors, of any zero-sum game without a pure saddle point, is a mixed strategy (Nash 1950); randomized algorithms beat deterministic ones on adversarial inputs; randomized controlled trials exist because randomizing the action is what makes the inference valid. The essay reaches its slogan ("a random key does not open a random lock") from a single-agent card task with a stationary distribution, then extends it to "an opponent who breaks those laws," where the conclusion reverses. "Lawful" thought against an adversary is a law that tells you to flip a coin.

The theories of AI that survived are the ones the essay's principle would refute. Stochastic gradient descent, the training procedure behind every large model, deliberately injects randomness into optimization (Robbins & Monro 1951); dropout randomly disables units to regularize; language models sample their outputs at a temperature above zero because greedy decoding produces worse text; exploration in reinforcement learning is randomized because deterministic policies get stuck. "Randomizing your actions takes you further from the target" is false as a general claim about optimization under uncertainty, and the subsequent history of the author's own field is the counterexample. The card task supports a narrow point about i.i.d. prediction; the essay generalizes it to a philosophy.
